--- title: 'Week 2: Python fundamentals I' --- [Open in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/github/WSU-EconS431/site/blob/main/weeks/week02.ipynb) · [View on GitHub](https://github.com/WSU-EconS431/site/blob/main/weeks/week02.ipynb) Last week Python solved a market from a formula we already knew. This week covers the pieces that let you write that kind of code yourself: values and names, decisions, repetition, and functions. By the end of the notebook you will solve an equation that has no tidy formula, using a method you write in about ten lines. **After this week you can:** - store numbers, text, lists, and named parameters, and print them readably - make a calculation depend on a condition with `if` / `elif` / `else` - repeat a calculation over many values with a `for` loop, and until a goal is met with a `while` loop - package a calculation as a function with inputs and a return value - read a traceback, find a bug, and use an AI chat assistant to help without handing it your thinking Run each cell in order (Shift+Enter). Change numbers and rerun; that is how this notebook is meant to be read. ## 1. Values, types, and names A **variable** is a name attached to a value. `=` means *assign*, not *equals*: the right side is computed first, then the name on the left points to the result. ::: {#c003 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} price = 12.50 quantity = 40 firm = "Palouse Lentil Co." competitive = True revenue = price * quantity print(revenue) print(type(price), type(quantity), type(firm), type(competitive)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 500.0 ``` ::: ::: The four basic types are `float` (decimal numbers), `int` (whole numbers), `str` (text), and `bool` (`True`/`False`). Multiplying a float by an int gives a float. Because the right side is computed first, a name can appear on both sides: ::: {#c005 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} quantity = quantity + 5 # take the old value, add 5, store the result under the same name quantity += 5 # shorthand for the same thing quantity ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 50 ``` ::: ::: **Floats are approximations.** Computers store most decimals in binary, so tiny rounding errors appear. Never test two floats for exact equality; check whether they are within a tolerance. Every numerical solver in this course stops at a tolerance for the same reason. ::: {#c007 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3) print(0.1 + 0.2) print(abs((0.1 + 0.2) - 0.3) < 1e-12) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` False 0.30000000000000004 True ``` ::: ::: ### Lists and dictionaries A **list** holds values in order; positions start at **0**. A **dictionary** stores values under names, which is a convenient way to keep a model's parameters together. ::: {#c009 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} prices = [2.0, 2.5, 3.0, 3.5] print(prices[0], prices[-1], len(prices)) # first, last, how many params = {"a": 100, "b": 2, "c": 10, "d": 1} print(params["a"], params["d"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 2.0 3.5 4 100 1 ``` ::: ::: ### Printing readably An **f-string** (a string starting with `f`) puts values inside text. The part after `:` controls the format: `.2f` means two decimals, `,` adds thousands separators. ::: {#c011 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(f"{firm} earns ${price * quantity:,.2f} selling {quantity} units.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Palouse Lentil Co. earns $625.00 selling 50 units. ``` ::: ::: ## 2. Making decisions: `if`, `elif`, `else` A price ceiling matters only if it is set below the equilibrium price. Code makes that decision with `if`: ::: {#c013 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} p_star = 30 # equilibrium price from Week 1 ceiling = 25 if ceiling < p_star: print(f"The ceiling binds: price is held at {ceiling}.") else: print(f"The ceiling does not bind: price stays at {p_star}.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` The ceiling binds: price is held at 25. ``` ::: ::: **Indentation is part of the code.** The indented lines belong to the `if` or the `else`. Positron indents four spaces for you after a colon. | Comparison | Meaning | | Logic | Meaning | |---|---|---|---|---| | `==` | equal | | `and` | both true | | `!=` | not equal | | `or` | at least one true | | `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` | ordering | | `not` | flips true/false | Use `elif` ("else if") for more than two cases. Here we classify a price elasticity of demand: ::: {#c015 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} e = -0.6 if abs(e) > 1: label = "elastic" elif abs(e) < 1: label = "inelastic" else: label = "unit elastic" print(f"An elasticity of {e} is {label}.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` An elasticity of -0.6 is inelastic. ``` ::: ::: ## 3. Repeating work: `for` loops A `for` loop runs the indented block once for each item in a sequence. With linear demand $Q = a - bP$: ::: {#c017 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} a, b = 100, 2 for p in [10, 20, 30, 40]: q = a - b * p print(f"P = {p:>3}: Q = {q:>4}, revenue = {p * q:>5}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` P = 10: Q = 80, revenue = 800 P = 20: Q = 60, revenue = 1200 P = 30: Q = 40, revenue = 1200 P = 40: Q = 20, revenue = 800 ``` ::: ::: `range(start, stop)` produces whole numbers from `start` up to, **but not including**, `stop`. A common pattern is to keep track of the best value found so far. This loop finds the revenue-maximizing whole-number price: ::: {#c019 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} best_p, best_rev = None, -1 for p in range(0, 51): # 0, 1, ..., 50 rev = p * (a - b * p) if rev > best_rev: best_p, best_rev = p, rev print(f"Revenue is highest at P = {best_p}, where it equals {best_rev}.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Revenue is highest at P = 25, where it equals 1250. ``` ::: ::: Check it with calculus: revenue $R = P(a - bP)$ has $dR/dP = a - 2bP = 0$ at $P = a/(2b) = 25$. The loop and the derivative agree. When a model has no closed-form answer, the loop still works; that is the main reason to compute. A **list comprehension** builds a list from a loop in one line: ::: {#c021 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} revenues = [p * (a - b * p) for p in range(0, 51)] print(max(revenues), revenues.index(max(revenues))) # largest value, and its position ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 1250 25 ``` ::: ::: ## 4. Repeating until done: `while` loops A `while` loop keeps going as long as its condition is true. Use it when you don't know in advance how many steps you need. How many years until savings double at 5% interest? ::: {#c023 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} balance, years = 1.0, 0 rate = 0.05 while balance < 2: balance = balance * (1 + rate) years += 1 print(f"{years} years (the rule of 70 says about {70 / (rate * 100):.0f})") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 15 years (the rule of 70 says about 14) ``` ::: ::: Make sure something inside the loop moves you toward ending it. If a cell runs forever, press the **Interrupt** (square stop) button at the top of the notebook, fix the loop, and rerun. ## 5. Functions A **function** gives a calculation a name, takes inputs (**parameters**), and hands back a result with `return`. Once written and tested, it can be reused with any inputs. ::: {#c026 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} def revenue(p, a, b): """Total revenue at price p when demand is Q = a - b*p.""" return p * (a - b * p) print(revenue(25, 100, 2)) print(revenue(25, a=120, b=3)) # arguments can be passed by name ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 1250 1125 ``` ::: ::: The text in triple quotes is a **docstring**. It says what the function does; hover over the function name in Positron to see it. **`return` is not `print`.** A function that only prints shows a number but gives back nothing (`None`), so you can't use its result in later calculations: ::: {#c028 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} def revenue_printed(p, a, b): print(p * (a - b * p)) x = revenue_printed(25, 100, 2) print("x is", x) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 1250 x is None ``` ::: ::: **Default values** let you leave out arguments that rarely change. This cost function has a fixed cost and a quadratic variable cost, $C(q) = F + cq^2$: ::: {#c030 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} def cost(q, fixed=200, c=0.5): """Total cost of producing q units.""" return fixed + c * q**2 print(cost(10), cost(10, fixed=0), cost(10, c=1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 250.0 50.0 300 ``` ::: ::: **Pass what a function needs as arguments.** Names created inside a function exist only inside it, and a function that quietly reads variables defined elsewhere in the notebook breaks when those change. That is why the PS1 functions take `a` and `b` as inputs. ## 6. Putting it together: solving an equation by bisection A firm sells at price $p = 40$ with cost $C(q) = 200 + 0.5q^2$. Profit is $\pi(q) = pq - C(q)$. What is the smallest quantity at which the firm breaks even ($\pi(q) = 0$)? **Bisection** needs only one fact: if profit is negative at `lo` and positive at `hi`, the break-even point lies between them. Check the midpoint, keep the half that still brackets the answer, and repeat until the bracket is tiny. ::: {#c033 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} def profit(q, p=40, fixed=200, c=0.5): """Profit at quantity q.""" return p * q - cost(q, fixed, c) print(profit(0), profit(20)) # negative, then positive: the answer is between 0 and 20 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` -200.0 400.0 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#c034 .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} lo, hi = 0.0, 20.0 tol = 1e-8 steps = 0 while hi - lo > tol: mid = (lo + hi) / 2 if profit(mid) < 0: # still losing money at mid: break-even is to the right lo = mid else: # making money at mid: break-even is to the left hi = mid steps += 1 q_be = (lo + hi) / 2 print(f"Break-even at q = {q_be:.6f} after {steps} halvings") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Break-even at q = 5.358984 after 31 halvings ``` ::: ::: Check against the quadratic formula: $0.5q^2 - 40q + 200 = 0$ gives $q = 40 - \sqrt{1200} \approx 5.358984$. Each halving cuts the bracket in two, so 31 steps shrink a width of 20 below $10^{-8}$. The `if` above works because profit rises on this bracket. A general version compares **signs** instead, so it works whichever way the function slopes. Functions can take other functions as inputs: ::: {#c036 .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} def bisect(f, lo, hi, tol=1e-8): """Return x in [lo, hi] with f(x) close to 0. f(lo) and f(hi) must differ in sign.""" if f(lo) * f(hi) > 0: raise ValueError("f(lo) and f(hi) must have opposite signs") while hi - lo > tol: mid = (lo + hi) / 2 if f(lo) * f(mid) <= 0: # sign change in the left half hi = mid else: # sign change in the right half lo = mid return (lo + hi) / 2 print(bisect(profit, 0, 20)) # first break-even point print(bisect(profit, 20, 100)) # profit turns negative again at high output ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 5.3589838510379195 74.64101614896208 ``` ::: ::: In Week 6 you'll use `scipy.optimize.brentq`, which does the same job in fewer steps. Now you know what's inside it. PS02 asks you to adapt this idea to find a market equilibrium. ## 7. Debugging Errors are normal; reading them is a skill. When a cell fails, Python prints a **traceback**: 1. **Read the last line first.** It names the error type and gives a message. 2. **Find the arrow** (`---->`). It points to the line that failed. 3. Fix that line, or the line that gave it a bad value, and rerun. Each cell below fails on purpose. If you use Run All, it may stop at the first one; run the rest of the notebook a cell at a time. ::: {#c039 .cell tags='["raises-exception"]' execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} revnue(25, 100, 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
NameError                                 Traceback (most recent call last)
Cell In[18], line 1
----> 1 revnue(25, 100, 2)

NameError: name 'revnue' is not defined
``` ::: ::: ::: `NameError`: Python doesn't know the name `revnue`. Usually a typo, or a cell defining the name hasn't been run yet (run cells from the top). ::: {#c041 .cell tags='["raises-exception"]' execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} revenue(25, 100) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
TypeError                                 Traceback (most recent call last)
Cell In[19], line 1
----> 1 revenue(25, 100)

TypeError: revenue() missing 1 required positional argument: 'b'
``` ::: ::: ::: `TypeError`: the function needs three arguments and got two. | Error | Usual cause | |---|---| | `NameError` | typo, or the defining cell wasn't run | | `TypeError` | wrong number or kind of arguments, e.g. adding text to a number | | `SyntaxError`, `IndentationError` | missing colon, bracket, or quote; inconsistent indentation | | `ZeroDivisionError` | dividing by zero, often at a corner of a model, such as zero quantity | | `IndexError`, `KeyError` | asking a list for a position it doesn't have, or a dictionary for a missing name | ### Bugs that don't raise errors The most dangerous bugs produce a number that looks fine. This demand function has the wrong sign and runs without complaint: ::: {#c043 .cell execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code} def demand_buggy(p, a, b): """Quantity demanded at price p.""" return a + b * p # should be a - b*p demand_buggy(10, 100, 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=20} ``` 120 ``` ::: ::: The defense is to test a case you can do in your head. An `assert` stops with an error if its condition is false, so a wrong function can't slip by. PS self-check cells work this way. ::: {#c045 .cell tags='["raises-exception"]' execution_count=21} ``` {.python .cell-code} assert demand_buggy(0, 100, 2) == 100 # passes: at P = 0 the sign doesn't matter assert demand_buggy(10, 100, 2) == 80, "demand should fall as price rises" ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
AssertionError                            Traceback (most recent call last)
Cell In[21], line 2
      1 assert demand_buggy(0, 100, 2) == 100              # passes: at P = 0 the sign doesn't matter
----> 2 assert demand_buggy(10, 100, 2) == 80, "demand should fall as price rises"

AssertionError: demand should fall as price rises
``` ::: ::: ::: ### Using an AI chat assistant to debug Through Week 5, chat assistants are allowed and inline autocomplete stays **off** (see [Policies](../policies.qmd)). A chat assistant is most useful when you ask it to *explain* rather than to *fix*: 1. Paste the **whole traceback** and the cell that failed. 2. Say what you **expected** to happen. 3. Ask: *"Explain what this error means and where my reasoning went wrong. Don't rewrite my code."* 4. Make the change yourself, rerun, and **check a case you know the answer to**. 5. Record what you asked and how you checked it in the AI usage note. Assistants are often confidently wrong about economics even when the code runs. Step 4 is the part that protects your grade. ## 8. In-class exercises Work with your lab partner. Each exercise has a check you can run. **E1.** Write `elasticity(p, a, b)` that returns the point price elasticity of linear demand, $\varepsilon = -bP/(a - bP)$. ::: {#c048 .cell execution_count=22} ``` {.python .cell-code} # E1: your code here ``` ::: ::: {#c049 .cell execution_count=23} ``` {.python .cell-code} # assert abs(elasticity(25, 100, 2) + 1) < 1e-12 # remove the # to check E1 ``` ::: **E2.** Loop over the prices 5, 10, ..., 45 and print each price with the label "elastic", "inelastic", or "unit elastic" (use your function from E1 and the `if`/`elif` pattern from Section 2). ::: {#c051 .cell execution_count=24} ``` {.python .cell-code} # E2: your code here ``` ::: **E3.** Use `bisect` to find the price at which the elasticity equals $-2$ when $a = 100$ and $b = 2$. Hint: you need a function that is zero at that price. Check: the answer is $2a/(3b)$. ::: {#c053 .cell execution_count=25} ``` {.python .cell-code} # E3: your code here ``` ::: ## This week - Read *Python Programming for Economics and Finance*: [3.
